title: Srikanth Saves Three Match Points and Outlasts Okimoto to Reach the US Open Final
excerpt: The former world No. 1 rallied from a game down to beat Japan’s Yudai Okimoto 22-20, 15-21, 21-19 in Fullerton, setting up a California title showdown with Chinese Taipei’s Su Li-yang on Sunday
body:
Kidambi Srikanth has reached the final of the US Open badminton tournament in Fullerton, California, after a pulsating semifinal victory over Japan’s fourth-seeded Yudai Okimoto on Saturday evening. The 33-year-old Indian, seeded fifth, won 22-20, 15-21, 21-19 in a match that stretched past an hour and required him to save match points in the decisive third game.

Srikanth will face Chinese Taipei’s eighth-seeded Su Li-yang in Sunday’s final at Court 1 of the Fullerton campus — a BWF Super 300 title match played out in the heart of Southern California’s Indian diaspora belt, barely 30 miles from the largest concentration of Indian Americans on the West Coast.

## A Decider That Went Down to the Wire

The semifinal began as a tactical arm wrestle. Srikanth edged the first game 22-20, converting on his fourth game point after Okimoto had clawed his way back from 15-18 down. The Japanese fourth seed seized the initiative in the second, levelling the match at 21-15 with more aggressive net play and fewer unforced errors.

The decider swung back and forth. Okimoto led at various stages and appeared to have the match within reach, but Srikanth — drawing on 15 years of international experience — lifted his intensity at the critical moments. He closed it out 21-19 as the Southern California crowd erupted.

It was the kind of comeback that defined Srikanth’s peak years, when he rose to world No. 1 in April 2018 and won four Superseries titles in a single calendar year. He may be ranked outside the top 30 now, but this week in Fullerton has shown he can still compete at the sharpest end of a BWF World Tour event.


![Yudai Okimoto — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/46/Okimoto_Yudai%E6%B2%96%E6%9C%AC%E5%84%AA%E5%A4%A7_%28cropped%29.jpg)



> **"Okimoto led at various stages and appeared to have the match within reach, but Srikanth — drawing on 15 years of international experience — lifted his intensity at the critical moments."**



## The Road Through Fullerton

Srikanth’s path to the final has been a masterclass in sustained excellence across five rounds. He opened by dispatching fellow Indian D. Saneeth 21-14, 21-12 in the first round, then produced his most eye-catching performance of the week in the round of 16 — a 21-14, 21-13 demolition of Malaysia’s Lee Zii Jia that sent a ripple through the draw. A quarterfinal win over Chinese Taipei’s Liao Jhuo-Fu (21-9, 12-21, 21-8) confirmed his pedigree in three-game encounters before Saturday’s showdown with Okimoto.

He has dropped only one game in straight sets all week, and each of his three-set matches has ended in his favour. His movement around the court — always his strongest suit — has looked sharper than at any point in 2026.

## Rounak’s Fairytale Ends One Round Short

The semifinal day began with heartbreak for 18-year-old Rounak Chouhan, the qualifier from Rajasthan whose astonishing run through the draw had been the breakout story of the tournament. Chouhan, ranked 80th in the world, had stunned top seed and world No. 6 Chou Tien-chen of Chinese Taipei in the second round with a come-from-behind 21-17, 26-24 victory — saving four game points in the process — before cruising past Israel’s Misha Zilberman 23-21, 21-11 in the quarterfinals.

But Su Li-yang proved a step too far. The eighth seed from Chinese Taipei controlled the rallies from the baseline and won 21-17, 21-19, denying the teenager a shot at an all-India final. Still, Chouhan leaves Fullerton with his first BWF World Tour Super 300 semifinal, a scalp that will echo across the circuit for months, and the clear signal that Indian badminton’s next generation is arriving faster than anyone expected.


![Southern California — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f3/Hermosa_Beach_Pier_I_%28262176665%29_%28cropped%29.jpeg)


## Devika Falls in Women’s Semifinal

In the women’s singles, India’s Devika Sihag — the Thailand Masters champion, seeded sixth — put up a fight against Denmark’s second-seeded Line Christophersen but fell 21-15, 11-21, 15-21 in a three-game semifinal. Sihag had been the last Indian woman standing after fifth-seeded Tanvi Sharma and Rakshitha Ramraj exited in the quarterfinals.

Sihag won the opening game comfortably but could not sustain the aggression, with Christophersen’s experience in the back end of BWF events proving decisive. Still, Sihag’s semifinal appearance marks a career-best result at a Super 300 event and continues a breakthrough 2026 season.

## What’s at Stake on Sunday

For Srikanth, the final against Su Li-yang offers more than just a title. It is a chance to prove that a former world No. 1 can still win on the BWF World Tour in his mid-thirties, at a time when Indian badminton’s youth pipeline — exemplified by Chouhan this very week — is beginning to push the older guard.

For the diaspora, the timing could not be better. The US Open is being played in Orange County, California, a region home to one of the largest Indian-American populations in the country. Local desi families who packed the stands this week for MLC cricket in Oakland and the FIFA World Cup across the state now have a chance to cheer an Indian athlete competing for a title on their own doorstep.

The men’s singles final is scheduled for Sunday afternoon at Court 1 in Fullerton.

*Sources: BWF World Tour, Sportradar, Badminton World Federation tournament data, IANS*
